_readme: NEW HAMPSHIRE -- Rules of the Superior Court of the State of New Hampshire
Applicable in Civil Actions. 13 rules, 35th computing jurisdiction.
*** THERE IS NO MAILED-SERVICE EXTENSION. NOT A SHORTER ONE -- NONE. ***
Every seeded jurisdiction until now has had one: the FRCP family adds three,
South Carolina and New Jersey add five, Hawaiʻi adds two, California and New
York use per-method tables. New Hampshire has NO such provision anywhere in
the civil rules or in the Supplemental Rules for Electronic Filing. The
phrases 'shall be added', 'additional days' and 'prescribed period' do not
occur; the ONLY sentence in the whole rule set matching a days-added shape
is Rule 26(b)'s deposition notice, which is a backward minimum and not an
extension. So NO ROW HERE CARRIES A service_extension FIELD, and a caller
passing service_method: 'mail' gets the identical date. A three-day
extension copied from any neighbour reports LATE on every New Hampshire
deadline -- the direction that loses a filing. A test asserts the field is
absent from all thirteen rows AND proves it as a date on every one.
AND THE REASON IS STRUCTURAL, NOT AN OVERSIGHT. New Hampshire runs its
periods from FILING and from THE DATE ON THE CLERK'S NOTICE, where the FRCP
family runs them from SERVICE. Rule 13(a) gives 10 days 'after FILING
thereof'; Rule 12(e) gives 10 days 'of the DATE ON THE WRITTEN NOTICE of the
order or decision, WHICH SHALL BE MAILED OR ELECTRONICALLY DELIVERED BY THE
CLERK ON THE DATE OF THE NOTICE'; Rule 43 gives 10 days 'from the date on
the court's written notice ... WHICH SHALL BE MAILED BY THE COURT ON THE
DATE OF THE NOTICE'. Each of those sentences names the delivery method and
then declines to let it matter. A rule that starts the clock on the day the
paper is sent has nothing to compensate for.
THIS IS A FIFTH ANSWER TO A QUESTION FOUR STATES ALREADY SPLIT ON. On the
post-motion trigger -- a party responding after notice of the court's action
-- Mississippi adds three (its Rule 6(e) reaches 'the service of a NOTICE or
other paper'), Hawaiʻi adds two (same words), Idaho adds nothing and
Nebraska adds nothing (both reach only 'after service'). New Hampshire adds
nothing for a THIRD reason again: there is no extension to reach the
question with, and the period does not run from service in the first place.
*** NO SHORT-PERIOD EXCLUSION, AND RULE 2 IS THE SHORTEST COMPUTATION RULE
ON THE PLATFORM. *** In full: 'In computing any period of time prescribed or
allowed by these rules, by order of court, or by applicable law, the day of
the act, event, or default after which the designated period of time begins
to run shall not be included. The last day of the period so computed shall
be included, unless it is a Saturday, Sunday, or a legal holiday, in which
event the period shall extend until the end of the next day that is not a
Saturday, Sunday, or a legal holiday as specified in RSA ch. 288, as
amended.' Two sentences. No intermediate-day exclusion (joins MN/UT/NV/KS/
ID/NE), no months-or-years rule, no hours rule, no backward-direction rule,
no subdivisions to cite. It matters more here than the tally suggests: FOUR
seeded rows are TEN days, which Arkansas's 14-day threshold and Alabama's
and Wisconsin's 11 would ALL exclude weekends from. The test asserts the
field is undefined rather than small.
THE HOLIDAY REFERENT NAMES A CHAPTER, NOT A SECTION, AND THAT DECIDED A DATE
IN HAWAIʻI. Rule 2 rolls off 'a legal holiday as specified in RSA CH. 288'.
Hawaiʻi's Rule 6(a) named HRS Sec. 8-1 alone, so the weekend-observance
section beside it fell outside the reference. Here RSA 288:2 is inside the
reference and is carried -- and RSA 288:2 IS A SUNDAY RULE ONLY. 4 July 2026
is a Saturday and New Hampshire has NO Friday 3 July observance, not as a
reading but because no clause could produce one. No RSA 288:1 holiday falls
on a Sunday in 2026, so the shift that does exist is dormant. See the
calendar file.
SOURCE, AND THE 403 IS NOT A WALL. courts.nh.gov returns 403 to a plain
curl AND to WebFetch, on every path including the homepage. It returns 200
with a full browser header set (Accept, Accept-Language, Sec-Fetch-*,
Upgrade-Insecure-Requests) -- 2,225,391 bytes, 228,837 characters of text,
all 55 civil rules plus 13A, 13B and 28A, complete and free. IT IS A HEADER
CHECK, NOT A GATE: no CAPTCHA, no terms page, no login. Colorado is a WALL
(CAPTCHA behind terms); New Mexico was an OBSTACLE needing a browser pass;
Idaho only had wrong guessed URLs. New Hampshire is a fourth shape again --
the document was always public and the request looked wrong.
*** THE PUBLISHED RULES CARRY NO AMENDMENT HISTORY AND NO EFFECTIVE DATES.
*** Hawaiʻi, Idaho, Nebraska and New Mexico all print bracketed amendment
notes on each rule. The New Hampshire Judicial Branch prints the rule text
and a Comment and nothing else -- checked on the combined page and on an
individual rule page. So every effective_from here comes from the ADOPTION
ORDER instead: the Supreme Court's order of 22 May 2013, whose own words are
'The amendments shall take effect October 1, 2013', and whose Appendix B
opens with a PREAMBLE -- 'They take effect on October 1, 2013, and apply to
civil actions pending or filed in superior court on or after that date' --
that the currently-published web version does not reproduce.
AND EVERY SEEDED ROW WAS DIFFED AGAINST THAT ORDER, NOT ASSUMED FROM IT.
The operative sentence of each row was searched for verbatim in the 2013
text. WITH ONE IMPORTANT LIMIT, RECORDED BECAUSE IT CHANGES WHAT THE DIFF
PROVES: the order's PDF text layer DROPS WORDS. Rule 43 comes back as '...a
motion to set aside any other verdict or decree shall be filed which shall
be mailed by the court...', missing the eleven words that carry the period.
So a hit proves PRESENCE and a miss proves NOTHING. Absence had to be
established from the order's TABLE OF CONTENTS, which is clean: it runs 1
through 54 with NO Rule 13A, NO Rule 13B, NO Rule 28A and NO Rule 55.
TWO ROWS WERE DROPPED FOR WANT OF A DATE, THE NEW MEXICO DISCIPLINE. Rule
13A's ten-day reply to an objection and its three-day notice to the clerk,
and Rule 12's thirty-day summary-judgment objection with its twenty-day
reply to an additional statement of material facts, are all real, current
and useful -- and all POST-DATE the 2013 adoption with no published
effective date anywhere on the Judicial Branch site. Seeding them would mean
inventing an effective_from. They are omitted and named here instead.
ONE SEEDED ROW CHANGED WORDING SINCE 2013 AND SAYS SO ON ITS FACE. Rule
28(a) as adopted required a party to FILE the request with the court and
DELIVER a copy, and ran the thirty days from that DELIVERY; the current text
says SERVE and runs from SERVICE. The number is identical in both and the
practical trigger is the same event. It is seeded with the current quote and
the 2013 date, and the row's note states the change rather than hiding it.
Rule 12(e) is the same shape and smaller: 2013 said 'A Motion for
Reconsideration or other post-decision relief SHALL BE FILED within 10 days
of the date on the written Notice', the current text says 'A party INTENDING
TO FILE ... SHALL DO SO within 10 days of the date on the written Notice'
and adds 'or electronically delivered'. Same ten days, same trigger,
verbatim.
ADMISSIONS ARE A PLAIN THIRTY DAYS -- NO FLOOR, NO ELECTION, AND THAT IS A
SHAPE NOT SEEN BEFORE HERE. Mississippi, New Mexico, South Carolina and
Hawaiʻi all make Rule 36 a later_of because the rule says a defendant 'shall
not be required to serve ... before the expiration of' forty-five days;
Kansas makes all three discovery rules elections; Nebraska's say 'whichever
is longer'; Idaho has no 45-day figure at all. New Hampshire's Rule 28(a)(i)
does something none of them do: it puts the protection on the REQUESTING
party's side instead. A request may be served only 'AFTER 30 DAYS AFTER the
date the defendant is served with the Summons and Complaint', and once
served the response is a flat thirty days. Same protection, opposite
mechanism -- and it means NO ROW IN THIS SEED IS A resolve_periods. The
stakes are the usual ones: Rule 28 is self-executing ('shall be deemed
admitted unless...'), so a later_of copied across from a neighbour would
tell a New Hampshire defendant the matter is not yet admitted when it
already is.
NO BACKWARD ROW IS SEEDED, AND NEW HAMPSHIRE HAS THE MOST INTERESTING ONE ON
THE PLATFORM. Rule 2 extends to 'the NEXT day' and says nothing about a
period measured before an event -- the Mississippi, Idaho, Nebraska and
Hawaiʻi shape, not New Mexico's. What is being left out: Rule 26(b), no
deposition notice is reasonable 'unless served AT LEAST 3 DAYS, EXCLUSIVE OF
THE DAY OF SERVICE AND THE DAY OF CAPTION, before the day on which they are
to be taken'. That period carries its OWN counting convention, excluding
both endpoints, which Rule 2 does not supply and this engine cannot express.
Also omitted: Rule 5(a)(8)'s dispositive motions 'not less than 120 days
prior to the trial date', Rule 5(a)(9)'s other pre-trial motions 'not later
than 14 days prior to trial', Rule 35's 14-day trial-management filings, and
Rule 40's 10-day notice to a next friend.
ALSO DELIBERATELY NOT SEEDED, each for a stated reason: Rule 9(e)'s 30-day
motion to dismiss challenging personal jurisdiction (it runs from the SAME
trigger as the Rule 4(e) answer row and would make that trigger ambiguous);
Rule 9(e)(1)-(3)'s answer deadlines running from Supreme Court notices
(appellate events this engine is not given); Rule 4(c)'s proof of service
'within 21 days of the COURT-ORDERED DEADLINE for service' (a date set by
the order itself); Rule 5's 75-day structuring conference and 20-day confer
obligation (both run from 'the Answer date', a court-managed date rather
than a filing); Rule 10(d)'s 30-day third-party action (the 2013 order
re-letters this subsection, so the citation cannot be given confidently for
any date before the undated re-lettering); Rule 23(k)(4)'s 10 days after an
objection is withdrawn or overruled (the trigger is an agreement between
counsel that leaves no record the engine can be handed); Rule 27's 30-day
expert disclosure 'within 30 days of a request BY THE OPPOSING PARTY, or in
accordance with any order of the court' (two governing sources, one of them
an order); Rule 29's conditional-default rows (they run from 'receiving
notice', a receipt date, not a sending date); and the Supplemental
Electronic Filing Rules' 'timely filed if it is filed BEFORE MIDNIGHT on the
date the filing is due', which is a moment and not a date -- the same thing
this engine could not express in New Mexico.

rules.label: Appearance and Answer after service of the Summons and Complaint -- 30 days (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: (e) Appearances and Answers are due within 30 days of the date the defendant is served with the Summons and Complaint.
authority.note: THIRTY, AND STATED TWICE. Rule 4(e) gives the figure directly and Rule 9(a) restates it from the other end -- 'An Answer or other responsive pleading shall be filed with the court within 30 days after the person filing said pleading has been served' -- and Rule 9(a) adds that 'within the same 30 days' an appearance must be filed too. Both sentences are verbatim in the 22 May 2013 adoption order. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, AND NOT BECAUSE OF A CARVE-OUT: New Hampshire has no mailed-service extension at all, in these rules or in the Supplemental Rules for Electronic Filing. Passing service_method changes nothing on this row or any other. NOT SEEDED ALONGSIDE IT: Rule 9(e)'s 30-day motion to dismiss challenging personal jurisdiction, sufficiency of process or sufficiency of service, which runs from this same trigger -- seeding it would make 'service_of_summons_and_complaint' match two rules and the engine would have to choose.

rules.label: Answer to a cross-claim -- 30 days (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: (a) An Answer or other responsive pleading shall be filed with the court within 30 days after the person filing said pleading has been served with the pleading to which the Answer or response is made.
authority.note: ONE GENERIC SENTENCE COVERS EVERY RESPONSIVE PLEADING, which is why this row and the counterclaim row share a citation. New Hampshire has no Rule 12(a)-style table of separate periods; Rule 9(a) is the whole of it and Rule 6(a) supplies the list of pleadings it can apply to -- 'a Complaint and an Answer; an Answer to a counterclaim denominated as such; an Answer to a cross-claim, if the Answer contains a cross-claim; a Third-Party Complaint ...; a Third-Party Answer ...; and a Reply, if an affirmative defense is set forth in an Answer'. THIRTY FOR ALL OF THEM, the way Mississippi uses thirty and Hawaiʻi uses twenty for all four of its Rule 12(a) periods. NO SERVICE EXTENSION EXISTS IN NEW HAMPSHIRE, so unlike Hawaiʻi -- where a mailed cross-claim collects two days and a mailed summons collects none -- these two rows behave identically under every service method.

rules.label: Answer to a counterclaim, from service of the Answer stating it -- 30 days (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: (a) An Answer or other responsive pleading shall be filed with the court within 30 days after the person filing said pleading has been served with the pleading to which the Answer or response is made.
authority.note: A COUNTERCLAIM IS PLEADED IN THE ANSWER, so the period runs from service of the Answer -- Rule 6(a) allows 'an Answer to a counterclaim DENOMINATED AS SUCH', and the pleading served is the Answer that contains it. THE WORD 'DENOMINATED' IS LOAD-BEARING: an Answer that does not denominate its claim as a counterclaim does not start this clock, and Rule 10(a) makes a counterclaim arising from the same transaction COMPULSORY, so the pleader who omits the label has a different problem. NO SERVICE EXTENSION EXISTS IN NEW HAMPSHIRE.

rules.label: Answer after a Motion to Dismiss is finally denied -- 30 days from the date on the Notice (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: If a Motion to Dismiss is submitted and denied, an Answer must be filed within 30 days after the date on the Notice of the Decision finally denying the motion; provided, however, that if a Motion to Dismiss which challenges the court's personal jurisdiction, the sufficiency of process and/or the sufficiency of service of process is filed, an Answer must be filed within the time specified in section (e) of this rule.
authority.note: THE TRIGGER IS THE DATE ON THE NOTICE, NOT THE DATE IT ARRIVES, AND THAT IS WHY THE SERVICE QUESTION NEVER ARISES. Four seeded jurisdictions split on this exact shape: on 'notice of the court's action' Mississippi adds three days (Rule 6(e) reaches 'the service of a NOTICE or other paper'), Hawaiʻi adds two (same words), Idaho adds nothing and Nebraska adds nothing (both reach only 'after service'). NEW HAMPSHIRE IS A FIFTH ANSWER AND A DIFFERENT KIND OF ANSWER: there is no extension provision in the rules to reach the question with, and the clock starts on the day the Notice is dated rather than on delivery, so nothing is being compensated for. 'FINALLY DENYING' IS NOT DECORATION: Rule 9(e) carves out motions challenging personal jurisdiction, process or service of process, whose answer deadlines run instead from Supreme Court notices under 9(e)(1)-(3) and are NOT seeded -- those are appellate events this engine is not given. The word 'submitted' rather than 'filed' is the rule's own; it is quoted as published.

rules.label: Objection or response to a motion -- 10 days from the FILING of the motion (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: (a) A non-moving party may object or otherwise respond to a motion within 10 days after filing thereof unless: (1) the party is responding to a Motion for Summary Judgment, see RSA 491:8-a; or (2) another deadline is established by court order.
authority.note: IT RUNS FROM FILING, NOT FROM SERVICE, AND THAT IS THE STRUCTURAL REASON NEW HAMPSHIRE NEEDS NO MAILING EXTENSION. Every FRCP-family analogue runs a response period from service of the motion and then compensates the responding party for transit; this one starts on the docket date and never mentions delivery. TEN DAYS COUNTS STRAIGHT THROUGH WEEKENDS AND HOLIDAYS -- Rule 2 has no intermediate-day exclusion at any length, where Arkansas would exclude below 14 and Alabama and Wisconsin below 11. THE TWO EXCEPTIONS ARE NOT MODELLED AND ONE OF THEM IS NOT SEEDABLE: a court-ordered deadline under (a)(2) is set by the order itself, and the summary-judgment path under (a)(1) is governed by RSA 491:8-a plus a Rule 12 paragraph that POST-DATES the 2013 adoption and carries no published effective date. A caller computing an objection deadline to a summary-judgment motion must not use this row.

rules.label: Motion for reconsideration or other post-decision relief -- 10 days from the date on the written Notice (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: A party intending to file a motion for reconsideration or to request other post-decision relief shall do so within 10 days of the date on the written Notice of the order or decision, which shall be mailed or electronically delivered by the clerk on the date of the Notice.
authority.note: THE RULE NAMES THE DELIVERY METHOD AND THEN DECLINES TO LET IT MATTER -- 'mailed OR ELECTRONICALLY DELIVERED by the clerk ON THE DATE OF THE NOTICE'. Both methods are treated identically because neither is what the clock runs from. THE WORDING CHANGED SINCE 2013 AND THE PERIOD DID NOT: the adoption order reads 'A Motion for Reconsideration or other post-decision relief SHALL BE FILED within 10 days of the date on the written Notice of the order or decision', without the electronic limb. Same ten days, same trigger, verbatim in the order; only the delivery words and the 'party intending to file' framing are new, and the amendment carries no published date, which is why the row keeps the adoption date and says so here. TEN DAYS IS ALSO A JURISDICTIONAL TRAP OF ITS OWN: the rule goes on to require that issues be raised here to preserve them for appeal, so this is a preservation deadline as well as a relief one.

rules.label: Answers to written interrogatories -- 30 days (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: (i) The party, who is served with interrogatories, shall serve his or her answers thereto, by mail or delivery in hand, upon the party propounding them within 30 days after service of such interrogatories. The parties may extend such time by written agreement.
authority.note: A FLAT THIRTY -- NO 45-DAY FLOOR, NO ELECTION. Kansas makes all three discovery rules elections, Mississippi and New Mexico make two elections and one floor, Nebraska's three are all 'whichever is longer', Idaho has no 45-day figure anywhere. New Hampshire has none either, and the reason is the same as Idaho's: an absence, not a reading. THE RULE MENTIONS MAIL TWICE AND ADDS NOTHING FOR IT -- 'by mail or delivery in hand' describes how the ANSWERS travel, not a period. This is the sentence most likely to be misread as a mailing provision by a reader looking for one. THE PARTIES MAY EXTEND BY WRITTEN AGREEMENT and the engine cannot see such an agreement; a stipulated extension governs and this row does not. Rule 23(b) separately caps interrogatories at 25, which is a limit on number rather than time and is not modelled. NOT SEEDED: Rule 23(k)(4)'s 10 days to answer after an objection is withdrawn by agreement of counsel or overruled -- the withdrawal is an agreement between counsel with no date the engine can be handed.

rules.label: Written response to a request for production -- 30 days (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: (2) The party upon whom the request is served shall serve a written response within 30 days after the service of the request. A shorter or longer time may be directed by the court or, in the absence of such an order, agreed to in writing by the parties.
authority.note: THE RESPONSE IS SEEDED, THE PRODUCTION IS NOT -- the inspection itself happens at 'a reasonable time, place, and manner' specified in the requesting party's own papers under Rule 24(b)(1), which is a date set by the parties. A SHORTER OR LONGER TIME MAY BE ORDERED OR AGREED, and neither is visible to the engine; where one exists it governs and this row does not. A SEPARATE THIRTY LIVES IN RULE 25 FOR ELECTRONICALLY STORED INFORMATION and is NOT seeded, because it runs from 'the RECEIPT of the request' rather than from service -- a receipt date the engine is not given, and the only place in these rules where the two are distinguished.

rules.label: Sworn denial or objection to a request for admission -- 30 days, or the matter is admitted (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: (a)(i) Any party, desiring to obtain admission of the signature on or the genuineness of any relevant document or of any relevant facts which he or she believes not to be in dispute, may, after 30 days after the date the defendant is served with the Summons and Complaint, without leave of court, serve an original request therefor, accompanied by any documents involved, to the adverse party or his or her representative. Each of the matters of which an admission is requested shall be deemed admitted unless within 30 days after such service the party requested serves a copy thereof to the party requesting such admission, or his or her attorney or non-attorney representative, either a sworn denial thereof or a written objection on the ground of privilege or that it is otherwise improper.
authority.note: A PLAIN THIRTY, AND THE PROTECTION SITS ON THE OTHER SIDE OF THE TRANSACTION. Mississippi, New Mexico, South Carolina and Hawaiʻi all make admissions a later_of because their Rule 36 says a defendant 'shall not be required to serve ... BEFORE THE EXPIRATION OF' forty-five days from the summons. New Hampshire protects the same defendant by forbidding the REQUEST: it may be served only 'AFTER 30 DAYS AFTER the date the defendant is served with the Summons and Complaint'. Once served, the response is a flat thirty. SAME PROTECTION, OPPOSITE MECHANISM, AND THE ARITHMETIC IS NOT THE SAME -- a later_of copied from a neighbour would give a New Hampshire defendant a date later than the rule allows on facts where the summons was recent, and the rule is SELF-EXECUTING ('shall be deemed admitted unless'), so the error tells a defendant the matter is still open when it has already been admitted. NO ROW IN THIS SEED IS A resolve_periods and this is the row where that matters. THE WORDING CHANGED SINCE 2013 AND THE NUMBER DID NOT: the adoption order required the requesting party to FILE the request with the court and DELIVER a copy, and ran the thirty days from that DELIVERY. Both figures are identical in the two versions and the practical trigger is the same event; the amendment to service carries no published effective date, which is why this row keeps the adoption date and states the change here rather than hiding it. NOT SEEDED: Rule 28(a)(ii)'s parallel thirty days for disputing signatures and endorsements, which runs from the date the defendant FILES an Answer and duplicates a sentence in Rule 37(c).

rules.label: Motion to set aside a jury verdict -- 10 days after its rendition (New Hampshire)

trigger_document.label: the date the jury RENDERED its verdict in open court
trigger_document.not_the: the date judgment was entered on that verdict, or the date the verdict was recorded

authority.quote: A motion to set aside a jury verdict shall be filed within 10 days after its rendition, and a motion to set aside any other verdict or decree shall be filed within 10 days from the date on the court's written notice with respect to same, which shall be mailed by the court on the date of the notice. In each case, the motion shall fully state all reasons and arguments relied on.
authority.note: ONE SENTENCE, TWO TRIGGERS, AND THE SPLIT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF SEEDING IT TWICE. A JURY verdict runs from its RENDITION -- the day it is returned in open court, when the parties are present and no notice is needed. ANY OTHER verdict or decree runs from THE DATE ON THE COURT'S WRITTEN NOTICE, because nobody was in the room. Same ten days, different clocks, and a caller who uses the wrong one is out by however long the court took to issue notice. NEW HAMPSHIRE HAS NO RULE 50/52/59 EQUIVALENT: this single rule does the work that four federal rules do, and there is no separate motion for a new trial, no motion to alter or amend, and no judgment-as-a-matter-of-law period in these rules. RULE 2 HAS NO NON-EXTENDABLE LIST EITHER -- Hawaiʻi's Rule 6(b) freezes six rules and reaches into the appellate rules, Idaho's 2.2(b)(3) freezes six, New Hampshire's Rule 2 says nothing about extension at all and Rule 1(d) lets the court waive ANY rule 'as good cause appears and as justice may require'.

rules.label: Motion to set aside a non-jury verdict or decree -- 10 days from the date on the court's written notice (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: A motion to set aside a jury verdict shall be filed within 10 days after its rendition, and a motion to set aside any other verdict or decree shall be filed within 10 days from the date on the court's written notice with respect to same, which shall be mailed by the court on the date of the notice. In each case, the motion shall fully state all reasons and arguments relied on.
authority.note: THE SIBLING OF THE JURY ROW, AND THE THIRD PLACE IN THIS SEED WHERE THE RULE NAMES MAILING AND THEN REFUSES TO LET IT COUNT: 'from THE DATE ON the court's written notice ..., WHICH SHALL BE MAILED BY THE COURT ON THE DATE OF THE NOTICE'. The notice is posted on the day it bears, so the ten days begin before it can possibly arrive, and there is no extension anywhere in these rules to give the time back. A practitioner who receives a New Hampshire notice on day three has seven days left, not ten -- which is exactly the arrangement a three-day mailing rule exists to soften elsewhere, and New Hampshire simply does not soften it. THIS ROW WAS DIFFED AGAINST THE 2013 ADOPTION ORDER AND THE ORDER'S PDF TEXT LAYER DROPS ELEVEN WORDS FROM IT, returning '...shall be filed which shall be mailed by the court...' -- which is why absence in that document was never treated as evidence of a later amendment, and the rule set's TABLE OF CONTENTS was used for that instead.

rules.label: Plaintiff's automatic disclosure -- 30 days after that defendant files an Answer (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: (b) Time for Disclosure. Unless the court orders otherwise, the disclosures required by Rule 22(a) shall be made as follows: (1) by the plaintiff, not later than 30 days after the defendant to whom the disclosure is being made has filed his or her Answer to the Complaint; and (2) by the defendant, not later than 60 days after the defendant making the disclosure has filed his or her Answer to the Complaint.
authority.note: AUTOMATIC DISCLOSURE WITH NO REQUEST BEHIND IT -- a deadline that runs whether or not anyone asks, which no other seeded jurisdiction's civil rules impose in this form. IT RUNS PER-DEFENDANT: 'the defendant TO WHOM THE DISCLOSURE IS BEING MADE has filed his or her Answer', so in a multi-defendant case the plaintiff has a different date for each one and this row must be asked once per defendant. THE TRIGGER IS FILING, NOT SERVICE, like every other New Hampshire period. THIRTY FOR THE PLAINTIFF AND SIXTY FOR THE DEFENDANT IS DELIBERATE AND THE RULE'S OWN COMMENT EXPLAINS WHY: 'The plaintiff should have the benefit of the defendant's Answer before making its initial disclosure since the Answer will in all likelihood inform what facts are in dispute'. UNLESS THE COURT ORDERS OTHERWISE, which the engine cannot see; a structuring order under Rule 5 routinely does set these dates and then governs instead.

rules.label: Defendant's automatic disclosure -- 60 days after that defendant files its own Answer (New Hampshire)

authority.quote: (b) Time for Disclosure. Unless the court orders otherwise, the disclosures required by Rule 22(a) shall be made as follows: (1) by the plaintiff, not later than 30 days after the defendant to whom the disclosure is being made has filed his or her Answer to the Complaint; and (2) by the defendant, not later than 60 days after the defendant making the disclosure has filed his or her Answer to the Complaint.
authority.note: THE ONLY SIXTY-DAY PERIOD IN THIS SEED, and the two limbs are separated by a single phrase that decides whose Answer starts the clock: the plaintiff's thirty runs from the Answer of 'the defendant TO WHOM the disclosure is being made', the defendant's sixty from the Answer of 'the defendant MAKING the disclosure'. In a one-defendant case both dates come off the same filing and the two rows differ only by their length; in a multi-defendant case they come off different filings and using one trigger for both is wrong. SAME EVENT NAME WOULD HAVE HIDDEN THAT, which is why the two rows carry distinct trigger events rather than one shared 'filing_of_the_answer'. UNLESS THE COURT ORDERS OTHERWISE -- a Rule 5 structuring order routinely resets these and then governs instead.
